source.value:
First, we rewrite the numerator of the first term using $1-{cos}^{2}⁡x={sin}^{2}⁡x.$

$$
\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡x}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-1=\frac{1-{cos}^{2}⁡x}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-1
$$

Next, we factor the numerator of the first term as a difference of squares, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-{cos}^{2}⁡x}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-1 & =\frac{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}-1 \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x)}{\cancel{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡x}}-1 \\  & =\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{1}-1 \\  & =1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

source.question: q-141281
source.value:
Recall the sum formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v+\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

Applying the sum formula for sine with $u=x$ and $v=\frac{2\pi }{3},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+\frac{2\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2}+\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

source.question: q-65502
source.value:
First, we recall the sum formula for cosine:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(u+v)=\operatorname{cos}⁡u\operatorname{cos}⁡v-\operatorname{sin}⁡u\operatorname{sin}⁡v
$$

Applying the sum formula for cosine with $u=x$ and $v=\frac{2\pi }{3}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+\frac{2\pi }{3}) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡x\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡x+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

authoring.value:
Recall that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int csc⁡xcot⁡x\,\text{d}x & =-csc⁡x+C \\ \int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =tan⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int ({sec}^{2}⁡x-2csc⁡xcot⁡x)\,\text{d}x & =\int {sec}^{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x-2\int csc⁡xcot⁡x\,\text{d}x \\  & =tan⁡x-2(-csc⁡x)+C \\  & =tan⁡x+2csc⁡x+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

decisions.question: q-21026

source.question: q-21026
source.value:
The function is strictly increasing where ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$ Differentiating $f(x),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =2\cdot 3{x}^{2}-3\cdot 2x \\  & =6{x}^{2}-6x,\end{aligned}
$$

so we need to solve the inequality

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}^{2}-6x & >0.\end{aligned}
$$

The above inequality factors as

$$
6x(x-1)>0.
$$

The graph of $y=6x(x-1)$ has roots at $x=0$ and $x=1,$ as shown below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14035241/assets/ec7ea6baa82d60a6cf472c904460190042d889d86cb092b19d9809111bd93b36.png)

Therefore, we conclude that the function is strictly increasing on the intervals $x\in (-\infty ,0)\cup (1,\infty ).$

source.question: q-73670
source.value:
Let's introduce the new variable $u={2}^{z}-9.$ Differentiating gives 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}z}={2}^{z}\operatorname{ln}⁡2\,⟹\,\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\,\text{d}u={2}^{z}\,\text{d}z.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{2}^{z}}{\sqrt{{2}^{z}-9}}\,\text{d}z & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{2}^{z}-9}}\cdot {2}^{z}\,\text{d}z \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {u}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\cdot \frac{{u}^{1/2}}{(\frac{1}{2})} \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{{2}^{z}-9}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
